Athletes completed both the APSQ (Step 1) and all Step 2 questionnaires, regardless of their APSQ score. Step 2 questionnaires included the Patient Health Questionnaire -9 (PHQ-9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire (ASSQ), CAGE-AID for drug use, Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C), Brief Eating Disorder in Athletes Questionnaire (BEDA -Q), and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). All questionnaires were scored and marked as “flag” or “no flag” according to established t hresholds. Classification performance metrics were calculated and compared to previous literature. An exploratory factor analysis was conducted to inve stigate covariance between Step 2 questionnaires and explain observed false negative rates (FNRs). RESULTS: The prevalence of a flagged APSQ was 24.7%. Triplett, Amber T. Donaldson, FACSM, Jonathan T. Finnoff, FACSM, Eric G. Post, William M. Adams, FACSM. United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee, Colorado Springs, CO. (Sponsor: Gregory D. Myer, FACSM) Email: travis.anderson@usopc.org (No relevant relationships reported) PURPOSE: To assess previous sample representation limitations and provide classification performance metrics to evaluate the accuracy of the Athlete P sychological Strain Questionnaire (APSQ) in triaging athletes to Step 2 of the Sport Mental Health Assessment Tool (SMHAT -1). METHODS: Prior to the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games, Team USA athletes (n= 911, age: 27.3±6.1 years, 52.1% female, 26.1% Par alympic) completed the SMHAT-1 as part of a mandatory pre-Games health screening. Athletes completed both the APSQ (Step 1) and all Step 2 questionnaires, regardless of their APSQ score. Step 2 questionnaires included the Patient Health Questionnaire -9 (PHQ-9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire (ASSQ), CAGE-AID for drug use, Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C), Brief Eating Disorder in Athletes Questionnaire (BEDA -Q), and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). All questionnaires were scored and marked as “flag” or “no flag” according to established t hresholds. Classification performance metrics were calculated and compared to previous literature. An exploratory factor analysis was conducted to inve stigate covariance between Step 2 questionnaires and explain observed false negative rates (FNRs). RESULTS: The prevalence of a flagged APSQ was 24.7%. FNRs were calculated as PHQ9=0% GAD7= 7.7%, ASSQ=52.9%, AUDIT -C=61.2%, CAGE- AID=37.5%, BEDA-Q=63.16%, PTSD=11.1%, congruent with previous findings. Exploratory factor analysis showed that GAD -7 and PHQ-9 were grouped under the first factor, while CAGE-AID was grouped under the second factor. The other questionnaires did not fit distinctly into either factor, suggesting the S MAHT is assessing a broad spectrum of mental health factors, which would be difficult for a single gene ric screening tool to triage adequately. CONCLUSIONS: While the SMHAT-1 remains an essential tool for athlete mental health screening, the high FNRs indicate limitations in using the APSQ as an initial triage instrument. The APSQ may be better suited as a Step 2 assessment. A bespoke Step 1 screening tool that captures the diverse spectrum of mental health concerns in athletes should be considered to enhance the tool’s effectiveness and potentially increase its adoption across al l levels of sport.
